problem: Existing VLN formulations rely on simplifying assumptions: text-only instructions, static obstruction-free environments, single-pass execution without adaptation, and fragmented treatment of exploration, representation and navigation.
motivation: These assumptions limit the applicability of VLN agents in realistic open-world settings. The thesis reformulates VLN under more realistic conditions to improve generalisability and robustness of embodied agents.
key_idea: Reformulate VLN under realistic conditions (multimodal prompts, dynamic obstructions, continual adaptation, unified 3D scene understanding) through new tasks, benchmarks and methods.
insight: From the abstract only: visual cues used in human navigation reduce grounding ambiguity and improve instruction following. Curriculum training with virtual graph construction keeps agents robust when instructions and reality diverge, and memory-based graph techniques improve performance over time. No ablation details are available because only the abstract was provided.
method: Multimodal-prompt VLN: extends instructions with visual cues, supported by multiple datasets and an integration module
Obstructed VLN: adds unexpected obstructions to static environments; uses curriculum training and virtual graph construction for robustness
Continual-adaptation VLN: a setting for adaptation to specific environments and user instruction styles; uses memory-based graph techniques
3D scene understanding benchmark: unifies exploration, representation and navigation in one pipeline
Baseline framework: dual-sighted exploration with LLM-based reasoning

setting.backbone: not specified in the abstract (includes LLM-based reasoning in the baseline framework)
setting.training_data: not specified in the abstract (new multimodal-prompt datasets and benchmarks introduced)

results: The abstract gives no quantitative results. It claims that multimodal prompts reduce grounding ambiguity and improve instruction following, and that the proposed methods improve robustness and long-term performance.
limitations: Abstract only, so no quantitative evaluation or implementation details are available
